rationale: Sacred inherited office provides context for the new king rather than a specific causal claim about Maurepas.
basis: The inherited sacred office frames Louis’s duties and preparation on pp. 1/43; changing the old Maurepas endpoint is justified, since ritual did not cause that appointment.

rationale: Distinct overlapping jurisdictions and legal-fiscal variety.
basis: The prose on pp. 2/4 describes distinct overlapping jurisdictions and legal/fiscal diversity; pairing avoids false causation and requires no map internals.

rationale: Institutional and geographic diversity interact; no single-direction explanation asserted.
basis: The source relates institutional fragmentation to uneven integration on pp. 4–5/9; weaker related-to wording appropriately avoids a single sufficient explanation.

rationale: Feudal incidence varies with tenure.
basis: Pages 11–12 qualify aggregate agrarian burdens through different tenure and seigneurial incidence; direction is correct.

rationale: Harvest fluctuation affects rural purchasing power and therefore industrial demand, not the existence or growth of rural industry in every respect.
basis: Pages 12–13 explicitly link harvest income and rural purchasing power to industrial demand; the restricted demand relation is more accurate than explaining all industrial growth.

rationale: Precarious work produces survival strategies.
basis: Pages 14–16 explain survival practices through poverty, precarious work and household pressure; direction and grouped outcomes fit the source.

rationale: Village solidarity coexists with internal hierarchy.
basis: Pages 16–17 show common rights and village solidarity coexisting with curés and dominant wealthy peasants; local hierarchy qualifies a homogeneous community view.

rationale: Factory organization differs from dispersed production.
basis: Pages 12/20 compare dispersed rural production and disciplined factory organization; the contrast applies to these aspects of the composite parents.

rationale: Subsistence mobilization extends beyond craft disputes.
basis: Pages 20–22 distinguish craft solidarity from broader subsistence action; related-to preserves interaction without making one identical to the other.

rationale: Legal order does not imply uniform wealth.
basis: Pages 27–29 expressly distinguish noble legal privilege from highly unequal wealth and power; the qualifier has the correct direction.

rationale: Maupeou and restoration respond to court opposition.
basis: Pages 37–39 make suppression and later restoration responses to the political role of sovereign courts; responds-to is more accurate than an inclusion hierarchy.

rationale: Robe administration relies on financier credit.
basis: Pages 40–41 connect robe administration and financier credit without identity; the undirected relation is sound.

rationale: Experienced minister guides inexperienced king.
basis: Pages 42–43 explain experienced Maurepas guiding the unprepared king; supports is personnel guidance, not proof of effectiveness.

rationale: French literacy opens a transnational audience.
basis: Pages 44–45 connect French linguistic reach with cross-border readership and periodical circulation.

rationale: Press growth supplies channels for opinion.
basis: Pages 45–46/56 supply print channels for a widening informed public; the direction supports opinion without claiming print alone created it.

rationale: Porous licensing and notoriety enable circulation.
basis: Pages 46/51–52 describe porous licensing, tacit protection and notoriety aiding encyclopedic publication and reception; qualified support preserves the censorship paradox.

rationale: Public access remains economically and socially bounded.
basis: Pages 47–48/56 show the public economically and socially bounded despite expanded access; qualifies is more precise than an unqualified expansion claim.

rationale: Voltaire campaigns against injustice and for judicial reform; a composite target containing miscarriages of justice must not make the edge read as advocacy of miscarriages or torture.
basis: Pages 55–56 concern campaigning against injustice and for penal reform; the narrowed verb correctly avoids advocacy of torture or miscarriages.

rationale: Intermediary powers shape anti-despotism language.
basis: Pages 50–51/59 connect intermediary powers with anti-despotism remedies; the current endpoint properly concerns checks on authority, not a claim that Montesquieu caused Maupeou’s attack.

rationale: Rousseau contests progressive orthodoxy.
basis: Pages 52–53 explicitly place Rousseau’s criticism of progress against progressive Enlightenment confidence; challenge direction is correct.

rationale: Justice campaigns organize public opinion.
basis: Pages 55–56 make campaigns over justice an important mobilizer of public judgment; the composite source is understood through campaigns, not torture acting independently.

rationale: Grain freedom tests agrarian doctrine.
basis: Pages 57–58 identify grain freedom as a policy application/test of physiocratic doctrine; direction and treatment are accurate.

rationale: Subsistence controversy deepens loss of confidence; does not undermine the collapse.
basis: Pages 58–59 make scarcity and famine-pact controversy contributors to distrust; the corrected contributes-to verb avoids the old inverse claim that they undermined the collapse.

rationale: Reputational damage weakens court authority.
basis: Page 60 develops court/queen reputational damage as a source of lost monarchical confidence; retained as a later episode, not backdated to 1770.

rationale: Unaccountable administration encourages representative remedies.
basis: Page 61 explains demand for representation as a response to unaccountable intendants; reciprocal old alternatives are safely consolidated in this directed remedy relation.

rationale: Necker relies on public confidence with limits.
basis: Page 62 explicitly describes Necker’s reliance on public confidence and its limits; uses has the proper agent and object.

rationale: Franklin makes the American example vivid.
basis: Pages 63–64 make Franklin’s image a vehicle for French admiration of America; popularizes does not assert perfect knowledge of American society.

rationale: Shared educated membership links sociability.
basis: Page 65 connects overlapping educated membership and parallel sociability; related-to avoids treating Freemasonry as a branch of literary societies.

rationale: Critical conclusion identifies credulity without erasing improvement.
basis: Pages 64–65 qualify rational improvement with credulity and easy-solution hopes; the correction removes the older unsupported America endpoint.

rationale: War accelerates accumulated financial pressures.
basis: Pages 66–68 make American war borrowing an accelerator of accumulated financial weakness; contributes-to preserves multiple causes.

rationale: Refused advances bring payment suspension.
basis: Pages 84–85 make refusal of further advances the immediate payment-suspension mechanism; the current relation is supported, while political-legitimacy consequences need the separately retained parent argument.

rationale: Notables assessed proposed reforms; submission was not implementation.
basis: Pages 70–72 document submission for endorsement and scrutiny, not implementation through Notables; the revised verb is correct.

rationale: Atlantic growth qualifies the wider economic picture.
basis: Pages 13–14 make Atlantic prosperity one component of the coastal/interior synthesis, not a contrast to the whole synthesis that already includes it. Old edges were inclusion/synthesis, and the current type obscures that logic.
proposed_fix: Use contributes_to_synthesis or is_component_of from Atlantic growth to the dual-economy subject; if contrast is wanted, target specifically the interior stagnation facet.

rationale: Unequal Church hierarchy produces clerical grievances.
basis: Pages 34–36 contrast hierarchy with underpaid parish clergy but also give inequality as a cause of grievance; the endpoint is a grievance/revolt process, and the rationale asserts causation while the type states contrast.
proposed_fix: Use contributes_to for hierarchy/patronage → clerical grievance, or rewrite the rationale to specify the actual comparative social positions and retain the causal mechanism explicitly.

rationale: Experimental reasoning makes scrutiny possible, without deterministic causation.
basis: Page 49 supports new scientific/experimental teaching as a contributor to critical reasoning; however the old mapped contrast between enduring classical/Catholic curriculum and Enlightenment improvement is a different qualification.
proposed_fix: Retain the current educational contribution only with an explicit bounded rationale, and preserve the curriculum-continuity qualification in the education parent or a separate qualifies edge; do not mark the old contrast semantically preserved by contributes_to alone.

rationale: Failure exposes political incapacity alongside fiscal weakness.
basis: Pages 75/85 link failure to secure reform with exposed political incapacity and eventual fiscal collapse; contributes-to avoids treating Notables as its sole cause.

rationale: Remembered ordinary surplus makes deficit disclosure contentious.
basis: Pages 67/71–72 make the remembered ordinary surplus a source of distrust when deficits were disclosed; direction and audit endpoint are accurate.

rationale: Land-tax equality is one reform component.
basis: Page 69 identifies territorial subvention as a central component of Calonne’s plan; the narrower tax subject properly points into the program.

rationale: Assemblies administer proposed taxpayer assessment.
basis: Pages 69/71 support the proposed assessment assemblies as part of the plan; apply this link to that initial design, not every later provincial-estates demand in the composite parent.

rationale: Economic stimulation accompanies fiscal reform.
basis: Page 69 makes commercial/economic stimulation a separate component of the fiscal program; part-of direction is correct.

rationale: Five-year plan seeks credit and retrenchment.
basis: Pages 78–79 describe borrowing, retrenchment and projected recovery as Brienne’s response to fiscal weakness; the relation does not endorse his calculations.

rationale: Forced registration undermines likely approval.
basis: Pages 79–80 explain how imposed registration destroyed the prospect of consent and intensified conflict; trigger and direction are sound.

rationale: Institutional coercion meets broad resistance.
basis: Pages 82–83 develop broad resistance to the judicial coup across courts, privileged bodies and crowds; provokes is supported without assuming a uniform coalition.

rationale: Credit weakness constrains intervention.
basis: Pages 75/77–78 explicitly use Dutch nonintervention to reveal fiscal constraints; retain lost prestige as a consequence in the parent rather than substituting it for the current evidentiary direction.

rationale: Weather weakens expected tax receipts, not sole cause.
basis: Page 84 links expected harvest damage to poorer tax security and credit refusal; contributes-to correctly avoids a sole-cause weather explanation.

rationale: Scarcity increases July volatility, alongside political and military triggers.
basis: Pages 86–87/109 connect scarcity and government blame to volatility alongside military and political triggers; the narrowed July consequence is sound, not proof of all earlier popular intervention.

rationale: Treaty worsens existing depression but is not sole cause.
basis: Page 87 explicitly says the treaty aggravated an existing depression rather than creating it; the revised causal strength is appropriate.

rationale: Doubling does not settle voting.
basis: Page 93 makes doubling compatible with unresolved voting procedure; the edge correctly distinguishes representation numbers from head voting.

rationale: Verification conflict becomes unilateral sovereign claim.
basis: Pages 102–105 show verification deadlock becoming roll-call and a sovereign National Assembly claim; broader old Bailly biography is internal context, not an independently proved causal edge.

rationale: Galleries favor intransigence without being sole cause.
basis: Pages 103–104 show gallery pressure reinforcing intransigence; supports avoids reducing deputies’ action to crowd compulsion alone.

rationale: Guards bring expertise and cannon.
basis: Page 110 identifies experienced French Guards and cannon as enabling Bastille surrender; use this military contribution, not every Invalides event, as the link.

rationale: Dismissal and troops activate existing fear and scarcity.
basis: Pages 108–109 link troops and Necker’s dismissal with fear and activation of Paris crowds; precipitates retains existing scarcity and anxiety.

rationale: Victory and unreliable troops compel royal retreat.
basis: Pages 110–111 make the Bastille victory and army unreliability causes of royal retreat and Parisian guardianship; the contribution is supported.

rationale: Loss of enforceable royal authority opens the space for reconstruction.
basis: Pages 112/134–135 place institutional reconstruction after loss of enforceable royal resistance; enables does not imply that all later reforms were preplanned.

rationale: Countryside panic and attacks force deputies to act.
basis: Pages 115–116 link rural panic and attacks to deputies’ urgent concessions; precipitates has the right event and response.

rationale: Peasant action and expectations exceed the terms of redemption.
basis: Pages 115/117/128/130 show peasant expectations and nonpayment defeating redemption; the qualifier applies to legal limits within the composite decree/reality parent.

rationale: August decisions are translated into distinctions in law.
basis: Pages 116–117 describe renunciations translated into carefully qualified legal decrees; the chronological result relation is direct.

rationale: Already rejected binding instructions no longer confine reconstruction.
basis: Page 118 explains that binding mandates had already been rejected, enabling later reforms beyond instructions; page 135 confirms that substantive divergence. Do not date the rejection to the later August debate.

rationale: The Declaration’s civil equality and rights language contrast with restricted political citizenship. Preserve the civil/political distinction; this is not a claim that equality of taxation itself confers the franchise.
basis: Pages 118–119/124–125 distinguish civil equality and natural rights from restricted political participation; the rationale properly removes any equation of fiscal equality with franchise.

rationale: King and Assembly move under closer Paris scrutiny.
basis: Pages 122–123 place king and Assembly under closer Parisian scrutiny after the October transfer; result direction is accurate.

rationale: Federation shows the breadth of temporary agreement.
basis: Pages 128/135 explicitly make the Federation a celebration and evidence of broad but temporary consensus.

rationale: Refusal adds to an inherited debt crisis.
basis: Pages 130–132 show tax refusal worsening inherited debt and immediate financing pressure; aggravates preserves the crisis’s prior existence.

rationale: Resistance and failed enforcement prompt the compulsory oath.
basis: Pages 143–144 make resistance and failed enforcement the immediate reason for the compulsory oath; the Civil Constitution is the antecedent settlement, not the oath itself.

rationale: Losses replace clerical goodwill with distrust.
basis: Pages 136–137 contrast early clerical goodwill with accumulating losses and distrust; contribution to consensus breakdown is direct.

rationale: Paris women act in the opposite religious direction, coercing refractory practice.
basis: Page 148 documents women coercing refractory worship; this is a specific participation claim, not a claim that women uniformly opposed Catholicism.

rationale: Formal religious freedom contrasts with coercion against nonjurors.
basis: Pages 137/146/148 contrast declared religious equality with attacks on nonjuror worship; institutional policy and crowd practice remain distinguishable.

rationale: Agricultural downturn and real-wage pressure deepen household insecurity; the relation concerns demand and livelihoods, not a claim that population caused individual crop failures.
basis: Pages 12/14–15 link agricultural downturn and demand with household insecurity; direction and guarded causal strength are appropriate.

rationale: Large commercial cultivators seek enclosure and concentrated use while villages defend collective grazing and other common rights; this is a conflict of uses, not a universal opposition between all farmers and all peasants.
basis: Pages 11–12/19 describe conflict over enclosure and communal usage; the rationale properly limits it to particular commercial cultivators and collective rights.

rationale: Naval selection and technical competence contrast with the army officer corps’s purchase, social distance and uneven professional access; restrict the comparison to recruitment and competence.
basis: Pages 30–33 contrast naval professional recruitment with army purchase/social distance; a bounded institutional comparison is supported.

rationale: Poor households’ expenditure on grain makes price rises dangerous and subsistence protest intelligible; precarious wages do not cause crop failure.
basis: Pages 14/20–21 explain how poor households’ grain dependence raises exposure to prices; it does not falsely make poverty cause crop failure.

rationale: Legal, clandestine and foreign book supply circulates the works and criticism associated with Enlightenment; censorship persists and circulation does not equate to universal assent.
basis: Pages 46–49 support circulation through licensed, clandestine and foreign books; the caveat that access is not universal assent preserves source stance.

rationale: Defeat encourages inquiry into institutions and the postwar search for improvement; failed reform and subsequent conflicts deepen the later confidence crisis. Defeat is one contributor, not a sufficient cause.
basis: Pages 56–59 connect defeat, inquiry, failed reforms and distrust; the causal contribution is supported and not sufficient by itself.

rationale: The postwar inquest makes economic improvement a ministerial priority and helps give Physiocratic ideas an audience.
basis: Pages 56–57 show postwar ministerial interest giving economic reform/Physiocracy an audience; the relation does not claim the war invented the doctrine.

rationale: The longstanding Jansenist conflict supplies the Nouvelles ecclésiastiques example within the expanding press; it does not explain all journalism.
basis: Pages 45/53–54 link Jansenist conflict to a specific clandestine press strand; the bounded verb avoids explaining all periodical growth.

rationale: Religious prosecutions and attacks help cohere the philosophes’ sense of common cause despite doctrinal differences; changing orthodox piety remains a separate facet.
basis: Pages 51/53–55 explain common purpose among diverse philosophes through harassment and opposition; the rationale separates changing piety from persecution.

rationale: Prolonged intra-Catholic conflict and changes in piety accompany declining acceptance of persecution. The source does not establish a single sufficient cause of toleration.
basis: Pages 53–55 connect religious tensions with changing attitudes toward persecution; provides-context is a warranted cautious relation.

rationale: Uncertain authority to consent raises demand for national body.
basis: Pages 72/74–75 support Notables’ uncertain authority promoting the national representative remedy. But mapped old consent↔credible accounts edges (B1BE49990719/C0FE84E2F96F) state an epistemic condition, not this institutional successor demand.
proposed_fix: Keep the current edge; preserve credible accounts as a condition of consent explicitly inside 7736E536CA42 and correct those old-edge dispositions to internalized rather than preserved by this edge. Keep Calonne’s initial preference for Notables over uncontrollable Estates as a distinct precursor.

rationale: Public mobilization reinforces resistance.
basis: Publicity supports court resistance on pp. 76–77, but old REL-060821A415BF is state repression responding to mobilization. It does not have the current endpoints or direction.
proposed_fix: Keep the current edge; mark the repression-response clue as internalized in the public-opinion/coercion treatment or preserve a properly directed independent edge if needed. Do not use support-for-Parlement as its semantic replacement.

rationale: Personal liberty and fundamental laws justify court opposition.
basis: Pages 80–81 show constitutional law and personal liberty justifying resistance, while the source subject also includes arbitrary arrest. Articulates is ambiguous when the subject is an issue rather than the Parlement or its spokesman. Old d’Epremesnil actor-within is not the same relation.
proposed_fix: Use provides_justification_for, with the fundamental-laws facet explicitly named; internalize d’Epremesnil’s leadership in the relevant parent rather than treating this as its preserved actor edge.

rationale: Vizille provides a modern alternative to 1614 forms.
basis: The source contrasts Vizille with 1614, but the current target itself contains the competing head-vote model, which Vizille exemplifies. A contrast to the entire target obscures agreement with its modern pole.
proposed_fix: Specify contrasts_with_1614_forms_within or instead exemplifies_head_voting_alternative_within, retaining Vizille’s support for doubling and common deliberation.

rationale: Society funds and organizes publicity without continued control.
basis: Society funding and organization support publicity on pp. 90–91, but old bourgeois-awakening and petition-organization claims are broader than a press route alone.
proposed_fix: Keep the current edge; ensure the political awakening/petition mechanism is explicit in parent 75B959BD3520 or connect the Society to the appropriate Third-estate mobilization requirement. Correct old mappings that claim the press edge alone preserves all outcomes.

rationale: Clerical cooperation does not erase Catholic institutional solidarity.
basis: The clerical-solidarity qualification is sound on pp. 99/104/107, but the very broad election parent also contains noble and electoral-rule arguments. Old representation part-of rules and liberal-noble support for union are not represented by this clerical qualifier.
proposed_fix: Name the clerical facet in the relation type/rationale and explicitly disposition old 19AA338D54A0 as internalized electoral structure; preserve liberal-noble union and clergy-defection causal contributions as separate parent statements or correctly scoped links, not this qualifier.

rationale: Adequate numbers do not guarantee discipline or obedience.
basis: French Guard unreliability contributed to the collapse on p. 110, but several old edges concern Broglie’s assessment of the army generally and withdrawal of royal troops, not this regiment alone.
proposed_fix: Retain the regiment’s contribution. Bind general army-unreliability/Broglie claims to the broader court counteroffensive or collapse parent, and do not claim that this narrowly sourced edge preserves the whole public-order dossier.

rationale: Bread scarcity combines with political fears and banquet reports.
basis: Bread scarcity contributes to the October action on pp. 121–122. The mapped old banquet/regiment-alarm edges are different political triggers, although the current rationale mentions them.
proposed_fix: Preserve banquet/counter-revolutionary alarm as an explicit independent factor in the October parent and correct the old mappings to internalized trigger claims rather than declaring them identical to bread scarcity.

rationale: Decentralized and weak administrative machinery impedes enforcement and collection under the new tax regime; it does not cause the egalitarian tax design.
basis: The new relation correctly restricts weak decentralized administration to tax enforcement on pp. 125–126/131–132. Old A348F429FD11 concerns the broader crisis of coercive authority, of which collection is one application.
proposed_fix: Keep this tax edge and explicitly retain broader enforcement weakness in the administrative/authority parent; do not mark the old general-coercion claim fully preserved solely through taxation.

rationale: Financial need gives force to the proposal for Church property.
basis: Pages 132–133 directly link failed financing to Church-land nationalization. Old 9B561EF0097A instead points from debt to assignat finance, a subsequent but distinct mechanism.
proposed_fix: Keep the current land-nationalization edge and bind the debt→assignat claim to a correctly scoped existing/new edge with the lead-owned assignat subject, or explicitly internalize it in a parent causal statement.

rationale: Cordeliers and Social Circle activists organize the petition preceding Champ de Mars; Lafayette and the National Guard implement the shooting. Petition organizers must not be labeled organizers of the massacre.
basis: The narrowed current type correctly makes these clubs organizers of petitioning, not the massacre. Old suppression-of-clubs edges and Lafayette/Guard implementation edges describe later effects or different agents.
proposed_fix: Retain organizes_petition_preceding. Preserve the reverse repression→club suppression in the parents or an explicit edge, and bind massacre implementation to Lafayette/Guard, never Cordeliers. Correct author mappings that treat these different directions as equivalent.

rationale: Some philanthropic lodges, including the Nine Sisters, engage in campaigns against judicial injustice; this is not institutional support for every literary society.
basis: Pages 55/65 support particular philanthropic lodges campaigning against judicial injustice. The revision corrects the old literary-society endpoint rather than claiming that all lodges pursued reform.

rationale: The argument for intermediary bodies and checks on despotism informs interest in accountable provincial representation, without making Necker’s programme a direct transcription of Montesquieu.
basis: Pages 51/59–61 connect intermediary-body ideas with the search for accountable provincial representation; informs-search avoids direct programme derivation.

rationale: Restored parlements fail to settle the confidence crisis, and representative provincial institutions become an alternative protection against administrative despotism.
basis: Pages 59–61 show restored courts failing to resolve distrust and interest shifting toward representative institutions; direction is supported.

rationale: State-led economic rationalization underlies enlightened administrative ambitions; arbitrary and unaccountable implementation creates opposition. This is contextual influence, not a claim that every intendant adopted the doctrine.
basis: Pages 57–58/60 place economic rationalization behind enlightened administrative ambitions while distinguishing arbitrary implementation; the contextual type is appropriately bounded.

rationale: Harvest fluctuation makes experiments in grain freedom politically vulnerable; distinguish shortage and subsistence unrest from the policy theory and conspiracy explanation.
basis: Page 12 dates renewed harvest uncertainty from the late 1760s, and p. 58 makes that same shift undermine grain-freedom optimism. The relation is to scarcity context, not a claim that later Louis XVI crop failures caused the 1763 decision.

rationale: Turgot warned against financing American intervention; Necker financed war through borrowing and cultivated public confidence. Compare fiscal strategies, not a personal quarrel.
basis: Pages 66–68 contrast Turgot’s warning against costly intervention with Necker’s loan/confidence financing. This compares fiscal strategies without inventing a personal dispute.

rationale: Calonne’s coordinated tax, provincial and commercial programme addresses structural fiscal weakness; it was proposed and contested, not implemented by the Notables.
basis: Pages 68–70 make the coordinated reform program a response to structural weakness; proposed and contested status is correctly retained.

rationale: Necker’s published account of financial administration and reputation sharpen doubts about Calonne’s management; limit the claim to reputation and the accounting controversy.
basis: Pages 69–71 connect Necker’s reputation/public financial writing to doubt about Calonne; the relation must refer to the accounting/reputation strand, not all loan finance.

rationale: The November 1787 Royal Session seeks registration of Brienne’s staged loan programme; a contested registration attempt is not successful implementation of the entire recovery plan.
basis: Pages 76–79 show the Royal Session seeking loan registration; seeks-authorization corrects the old misleading implementation verb.

rationale: Calls for the Estates-General increasingly make national consent the answer to taxation and credit problems, while the timing and political purpose of the demand change.
basis: Pages 71–84 track the Estates-General demand as a national-consent remedy while motives/timing change; the direction and limited status are correct.

rationale: The failure to enforce the May judicial settlement disrupts justice and tax collection and helps close the treasury’s remaining credit channels; retain debt and harvest damage as additional pressures.
basis: Pages 81–85 link failed judicial enforcement, tax disruption and refused credit to collapse, alongside other pressures; contributes-to is appropriate.

rationale: Treasury collapse leads to Necker’s recall because his public credit appears the only immediate remedy. It does not cause the Compte rendu published seven years earlier.
basis: Pages 84–85 connect bankruptcy with Necker’s recall because of public credit; the narrowed type avoids the absurd old implication that 1788 collapse caused the 1781 account.

rationale: The July hailstorm undermines tax and credit expectations already weakened by debt, anticipations and political resistance.
basis: Pages 83–84 show hail damage weakening anticipated receipts/credit, not independently producing all political collapse.

rationale: Treasury centralization threatens established financiers, whose refusal of final advances contributes to collapse; this is a particular administrative mechanism, not a claim that every element of Brienne’s plan failed identically.
basis: Pages 83–84 provide the specific treasury-centralization/financier-refusal mechanism; the bounded type preserves it without treating all Brienne reforms alike. His resulting fall is separately explicit in the bankruptcy parent.

rationale: Sieyes gives the third estate’s claim to embody the nation an influential anti-privilege formulation; the pamphlet is an intervention in an existing mobilization.
basis: Pages 93–94 make Sieyes’s pamphlet an influential expression of an existing national/anti-privilege claim; articulates is better than an exclusive origin claim.

rationale: Sieyes’s final appeal and roll call help turn verification deadlock into a claim of national representation; preserve the deputies’ collective action and broader constitutional setting.
basis: Pages 102–104 connect Sieyes’s appeal and roll-call with formation of national representation; contributes-to preserves collective agency.

rationale: The second Notables oppose doubling; the royal Result grants doubled third-estate representation while leaving voting procedure unresolved.
basis: Pages 91–92 contrast Notables’ rejection of doubling with the royal grant, leaving head voting unresolved; the comparison is direct.

rationale: Pamphlets and petitions enlarge anti-privilege mobilization and national claims; print is a means of publicity rather than a sufficient cause of social conflict.
basis: Pages 90–94 show publicity/petitioning widening anti-privilege mobilization; amplifies accurately preserves a means and effect without deterministic print causation.

rationale: Doubling the third estate without deciding voting procedure leaves the verification dispute capable of becoming a struggle over separate orders and national authority.
basis: The December doubling left head voting undecided (pp. 92–93), enabling the verification conflict on pp. 101–103. Add p. 93 to the evidence list for the explicit unresolved-procedure statement.

rationale: Necker’s equivocation at the opening offers no authoritative decision on the central procedural issue, leaving deputies to contest verification.
basis: Pages 101–102 show Necker failing to resolve the central issue at the opening; fails-to-resolve corrects older claims that equivocation alone caused verification.

rationale: Electoral assemblies prepare grievance lists alongside choosing deputies; electoral mobilization and cahier drafting are interlocking stages, not an abstract one-way cause of democratization.
basis: Pages 96–100 show grievance drafting and deputy election as linked stages. Noble/clerical cahier content remains required in the parent; preparation does not itself preserve each content-specific old edge.

rationale: Legal training equips leading third-estate deputies for the procedural dispute over verification and national legitimacy; it does not make their political outcome automatic.
basis: Pages 95–96/102–103 show legal training furnishing procedure while encouraging caution; the resources wording avoids an automatic lawyer-to-revolution inference.

rationale: Economic distress, high bread prices and shortages contribute to food disturbances during electoral mobilization; particular disturbances have local triggers.
basis: Pages 86–88/97–98 connect hardship with spring food disorders but preserve local triggers and an independent popular agenda.

rationale: Government procurement and contested trade rules form part of the supply context; do not flatten policy shifts and harvest shortage into a single cause of all bread politics.
basis: Pages 86–88/97/121–122 connect procurement/trade rules with supply and bread politics; the contextual verb avoids flattening different policy phases.

rationale: Troop concentration and Necker’s dismissal intensify fear of coercion and help prompt Paris electors’ militia preparations; the militia does not cause the earlier troop concentration.
basis: Pages 108–109 support court threat prompting defensive militia preparation; the current direction correctly reverses the false old claim that militia formation caused earlier troop concentration.

rationale: Scarcity and disorder contribute to provincial seizure and reconstitution of municipal power; Paris’s example, collapsing royal authority and local political motives also matter.
basis: Pages 113–114 connect scarcity/disorder to municipal seizure alongside Paris example and royal collapse; multiple causes are preserved.

rationale: Journalists and public agitation attack the Monarchiens’ constitutional proposals; the resulting suspensive veto is distinct from the full veto they advocated.
basis: Pages 119–121 show press/public opposition to an absolute veto; the wording confines the target to that proposal rather than opposing all suspensive-veto government.

rationale: Tax and property qualifications restrict political participation and eligibility for elective offices; the franchise limits the reach of election, not the reverse.
basis: Pages 124–125 show franchise/property thresholds limiting elective access; the corrected direction properly makes qualification constrain election.

rationale: The new direct-tax system’s weak enforcement and late collection aggravate the state’s financial crisis. Fiscal equality itself is not alleged to cause inherited debt.
basis: Pages 131–132 explicitly make weak collection worsen the financial crisis; the wording does not allege that equality created inherited debt.

rationale: State reorganization of the Church and the subsequent oath divide the earlier revolutionary coalition; distinguish the legal constitution from the later oath and regional reactions.
basis: Pages 139–143 begin the settlement-to-division process; the separate oath relation is necessary. Add pp. 144/157 if the current rationale continues to invoke the subsequent oath and final causal assessment.

rationale: Dispossession and loss of independent clerical resources place the Church increasingly in state dependence and make salaried reorganization possible; they do not alone cause every later schism.
basis: Pages 136–140 connect loss of resources with state dependence and salaried reorganization; the several old salary/expectation facets are internal parts of this process, not proof that property seizure alone caused schism.

rationale: Publication of the papal break and oath withdrawals intensify suspicion of refractory worshippers; popular persecution is not simply execution of papal policy.
basis: Page 146 directly connects publication, withdrawals and hostile action, with p. 148 later intimidation; the source does not make crowds instruments of papal policy.

rationale: The August press restriction belongs to the restrictive aftermath of Champ de Mars; it does not cause the shooting or retrospectively authorize it.
basis: Pages 154–155 place the press restriction in the aftermath of suppression; the time-specific type avoids backward causation.

rationale: Officer emigration worsens military leadership and cohesion later in 1791; it must not be projected backward as the cause of the earlier Nancy mutiny.
basis: Pages 147/156 distinguish Nancy’s earlier mutiny from later officer exodus and indiscipline; the bounded type preserves chronology and reciprocal deterioration.

rationale: French observers read American political language through ideas of liberty and popular authority familiar from French discussion, including Rousseau; this does not assert that Rousseau caused the American Revolution.
basis: Pages 63–64 explicitly connect Franklin’s imagined simple life with Rousseauistic virtue, while the American language of liberty/representation resonates with broader French anti-despotism. The rationale over-specifies Rousseau as the source of that political vocabulary.
proposed_fix: Rewrite as informs_idealized_simplicity_within, naming the Franklin/sylvan-virtue reception, or use only a general Enlightenment/political-discussion endpoint for liberty and representation. Do not infer a Rousseau-specific political influence from the thematic overlap.

rationale: Clerical, noble, provincial and popular resistance presses for representation; the groups’ motives differ and cannot be reduced to one revolutionary ideology.
basis: Resistance reinforcing demands for national representation is supported on pp. 81–84. Old REL-64EF183D1F55 concerns the government’s invitation intended to divide resistance—the reverse strategic action, not the current pressure.
proposed_fix: Keep the current edge and retain the divide-opposition purpose explicitly in the Estates-General parent or correct the old disposition to internalized; do not credit this edge as preserving that strategy.

rationale: Insistence on the 1614 order-based form turns a procedural and constitutional dispute into confrontation over privilege; it does not create the social orders.
basis: Pages 89–94 support procedural conflict intensifying anti-privilege confrontation. Old fiscal-equality versus order-vote distinction is not a causal equivalent of this relation.
proposed_fix: Keep the current edge; preserve the possible combination of fiscal equality with order-based political representation explicitly in the parent and correct old 1035E81C8A80’s mapping.

rationale: Citizens organize militias in response to weak policing and disorder as well as court threat; the relation is not militia creation causing the prior breakdown of enforcement.
basis: Weak policing and disorder prompt militia organization, but the source parent is explicitly June 1789 while the relation includes spring disturbances (97–98) and July preparation (108–109).
proposed_fix: Apply the already proposed broadening/reallocation of C918DFC81FAD before retaining this whole relation, or narrow the relation to the later Paris policing-to-militia sequence with appropriate source pages.

rationale: Direct action against seigneurial rights pressures the Assembly toward the night of renunciations; distinguish this pressure from the deputies’ legal qualifications and the continuing rural campaign.
basis: Pages 114–116 support direct action pressuring August renunciations. Old BAA6BC01FF0D instead says peasant action practically enforced abolition despite decree qualifications.
proposed_fix: Keep this pressure-before-legislation edge; bind the practical enforcement/nonpayment claim to the decree-and-social-reality qualifier REL-SUCC-A5940DD72EFB or explicit parent statement, not this earlier causal trigger.

rationale: Widespread evasion and resistance help make old indirect taxes and monopolies politically untenable, while reformers also act on egalitarian and economic principles.
basis: Pages 130–131 support tax resistance pressuring abolition alongside reform principles. Old 4862E62BBD26 instead concerns continuing nonpayment after replacement taxes.
proposed_fix: Keep the current pressure edge and explicitly preserve persistence under the new regime in the parent/collection-failure link; repair the lineage so before-reform pressure does not substitute for after-reform weakness.

rationale: Women act prominently in the October mobilization but remain excluded from the formal political franchise; retain this difference between popular intervention and legal citizenship.
basis: The contrast of women’s October action with exclusion from citizenship is source-supported. Old 6FBED98AB466 and 8403F386E613 concern popular guardianship and representative authority more generally, not this gender/franchise distinction.
proposed_fix: Retain the contrast; bind those two general intervention/authority edges to the October→Paris-guardian relationship or internalized parent explanation, not this narrower replacement.

rationale: The oath operates as a public test of allegiance and reveals, as well as deepens, the breach in consensus; an opinion-poll metaphor is not a separate causal mechanism.
basis: The causal/opinion-poll claim is supported on pp. 144–145 and in the synthesis on p. 157. The listed pp. 141–143 largely precede the oath and do not support the central public-choice/results claim. The old press-polarization edge is also broader than the oath.
proposed_fix: Replace evidence pages with 144,145,157 (143 only as immediate decision lead-in). Preserve conservative/patriotic press polarization on p. 142 explicitly in its coherent parent or separate relationship, not as an oath-only semantic equivalent.

rationale: Papal condemnation rejects the ecclesiastical settlement; distinguish delayed private opposition from publication and resulting oath withdrawals.
basis: The current unqualified condemns verb contradicts the parent’s careful stance and p. 146, which says the public letters stopped short of explicit condemnation although received as decisive. Private July warning is on p. 141, missing from the listed pages.
proposed_fix: Use opposes_and_is_received_as_condemnation_of, distinguish private schism warning from public letters, and cite pp. 141/146. Keep the publication-to-rupture sequence explicit; do not describe a simple formal condemnation.

rationale: Conflict over Avignon and the Comtat adds a territorial grievance to the ecclesiastical breach with Pius VI; the quarrels cannot be collapsed into a single doctrinal issue.
basis: The territorial-versus-ecclesiastical distinction is sound on pp. 139/146/157. Page 145 is oath geography/staffing, not papal enclaves; p. 138 only leads into papal concern.
proposed_fix: Use 139,146,157 for the developed territorial grievance and culminating annexation, preserving that Civil Constitution—not Avignon alone—was the decisive breaking point.

rationale: Republican petitioning challenges the Assembly’s preservation of monarchy and exposes divisions among former patriots; retain the precise dispute over restoration and national consent.
basis: The republican anti-restoration campaign on pp. 152–154 supports the current relation. Page 153 alone omits the final abdication/national-consent formulation on 154. Native REL-0081 concerned Champ de Mars as a response and is not this club→monarchy link.
proposed_fix: Add pp. 152/154; bind the petition→Feuillant split and later coercion to their actual explicit parent mechanisms/relations. Do not claim old massacre-response preservation through this different source and target.

rationale: The leaders’ move toward moderation and the fragmentation of earlier radical coalitions leave space for Robespierre’s distinct opposition and rise.
basis: Pages 149–151 clearly show moderation opening space for Robespierre. Old 5F32FF3F813E concerns his survival in the Jacobins after the later July split on p. 154, a different temporal relation.
proposed_fix: Keep the current relation and internalize the p. 154 survival fact explicitly in Robespierre/Jacobin parents, or add a separate post-split link; repair the old mapping.

rationale: Election and staffing of the Constitutional Church contrast with refusal and rival authority among refractories, with substantial regional variation.
basis: Constitutional careers and refractory refusal are contrasted on pp. 144–146. Listed 142–143 precede the defining oath/results and cannot carry the stated staffing contrast alone. Old oath-created-camps edges are causal definitions, not merely comparison.
proposed_fix: Cite 144–146. Preserve that the oath defines the two camps and that shortages force temporary use of refractories; add creates_camps or state this explicitly in both parents rather than declaring contrast alone preserves the causal definition.
